### page_1
Australian Journal of Earth Sciences (2000)47, 405–429
Towards a high resolution Late Palaeoproterozoic –
earliest Mesoproterozoic apparent polar wander path for
northern Australia
M. IDNURM*
Australian Geological Survey Organisation, PO Box 378 Canberra, ACT 2601, Australia.
Seven new primary poles upgrade the apparent polar wander path for northern Australia for the
period 1730–1590Ma. This brings the total number of primary poles to sixteen, of which nine have
well-defined SHRIMP U–Pb zircon ages. The upgraded path provides a tool for dating and correlation
of tectonic events as well as fluid migration episodes for one of the most important periods of base-
metal mineralisation in Australia. Other new primary and overprint poles allow the path to be extended
tentatively forward in time to ca1500Ma and back to ca1770Ma. The 1730–1590Ma path comprises
five quasilinear segments or tracks, each terminated by a sharp bend. The bends can be related to
major (supersequence) boundaries in the northern Australian superbasins and to the initiation of sub-
basins that host the base-metal deposits. Most bends are also associated with magnetic overprints
related to episodes of fluid circulation, and three appear to be associated with the expulsion of metal-
rich brines that formed the world-class Broken Hill, Mt Isa and HYC Pb–Zn deposits. According to the
pole path, the movement of the region in the period 1730–1590Ma can be described as series of
clockwise-counterclockwise rotations about mostly similar Euler poles located southwest of Australia,
suggesting that the lithosphere may have been coupled alternately to oppositely convecting cells
in the mantle. This mode of movement was terminated at the onset of the Isan Orogeny. The oldest
track spans a period of igneous activity from 1740Ma to 1710Ma that left a 1000km-long trail of
volcanics with a decreasing age trend to the northwest. Palaeomagnetic data are consistent with
the interpretation that this trail was caused by the movement of the plate over a thermal anomaly
in the upper mantle.
KEY WORDS: apparent polar wander path,McArthur Basin,Mt Isa Inlier,palaeomagnetism,Palaeo-
proterozoic.

AMOS FORMATION
The Amos Formation was sampled at its type section where
an ~80m-thick succession of red and grey siltstones and
sandstones grades upwards to massive dolostones,which
are capped by karst.Pink,redeposited tuffaceous beds in
the middle of the formation contain zircons dated by U–Pb
at 161464Ma (Page et al.2000).
A total of 88 samples was collected from benches of
resistant outcrop.Preference in sampling was placed on red

The formation was sampled at 17 sites within a broad origin for this remanence.First,the rhyodacite clasts in the
belt of scattered outcrop on the southern flank of the conglomerate deposited on top of the rhyodacitic Ptp5 have
Murphy Inlier where the volcanics are ~2km thick. The random remanence directions (Figure 8c),suggesting that
this lithology has not been overprinted. The clasts were
subjected to the same laboratory treatments and analysis

occurs between Ptp5 and Ptp6,again implying the absence
of blanket magnetic overprinting.The polarities in Ptp5 are
the same at the Wire and Walford Creeks sites and are oppo-
site to those in the other members.
Scarcity of unweathered outcrop, pervasive chemical
alteration,and difficulty in the absence of field relation-
ships of distinguishing the basalt flows from shallow
dolerite intrusives posed problems in the sampling of
Ptp1.The alteration is characterised by hematisation with
variable degrees of destruction of magnetite. Thermal
demagnetisation yielded three remanence components:B,
C and D.Component B with steep west downward dipping

This direction recurs throughout the overlying McNamara at the same locality as the Lochness Formation where only
Formation, and is therefore most likely an overprint. the lower parts of the volcanics, comprising mafic flows
In most samples its removal revealed a shallow east and interbedded siliciclastics,are found.Both rock types
were sampled. Also sampled were small remnants of a

A total of 74 red- and grey-brown samples was collected,
56 of these from the first locality.Thermal demagnetisation
yielded two components,A and B,that unblocked generally
between 680°C and 690°C and formed coherent directional
groups.Component A was found only in the interbedded
sediments,and its directions resemble closely those of com-
ponent A of the Lochness Formation.As noted above,the
Lochness component appears to be an overprint.
Component B (Figure 12a,b) was found in both the silici-
clastics and volcanics.Before tilt corrections its directions
for the two localities differed widely (Figure 12a).Although
tilt corrections did not produce coincidence,the directional
difference was greatly reduced (Figure 12b). While the
remaining discrepancy may be attributed to an age differ-
ence between the sampled units or to continued defor-
mation after magnetisation,it is more likely to be due to
an error in the bedding dip at the second locality.The fold
test is therefore considered to be positive.Because of the
uncertain bedding dip estimate at the second locality only
the directions from the first locality were used in the final
analysis.In calculating the overall mean direction for the

ESPERANZA FORMATION
The stromatolitic Esperanza Formation comprises mainly
siltstone and sandstone. Its thickness at the Gunpowder
Creek type section is 250m (Hutton & Wilson 1985).Ninety
samples were collected from stratigraphic sections at two
localities:Esperanza Waterhole (locality L23) and Mellish
Park (locality L24).Most samples were grey,some were tan
or red-brown.Both thermal and AF demagnetisation tech-
niques were used, but all except the red-brown samples
failed to give coherent directional groups. The latter
samples were collected mainly from a zone of joint-related
ferruginisation near the top of the Esperanza Waterhole
section and close to the Mt Gordon Fault.The directions,
shown in Figure 15,give a mean (declination 358.7°,inclin- Figure15 Esperanza Formation. Remanence directions from
ation –42.7°) that corresponds to the overprint OP4. hematised samples.Direction marked x was excluded from the
pole calculation.Symbols as in Figure 3.

Basin and Lawn Hill Platform,the Lawn Hill Platform poles
lying on the older part of the apparent polar wander path
segment.It should be noted that the 95% confidence circles
of the respective mean remanence directions do not
intersect (Figure 18a), confirming that the difference
between the pole groups is statistically significant. The
groups therefore seem to record two separate events,OP3A
(Lawn Hill Platform) and OP3 (McArthur Basin).
Comparison of the remanence directions before (Figure
18a) and after (Figure 18b) bedding corrections indicates
that OP3 and OP3A were acquired after the main phase of
deformation (D) in the Mt Isa Inlier.U–Pb ages of zircons
3
from two generations of pegmatite provide 153267Ma and
1480614Ma as the maximum and minimum age limits for
D (Connors & Page 1995).A possible explanation for the
3
OP3A/OP3 age difference is that hematite-bearing fluids
were mobilised by stresses in the late stages of the Isan
Orogeny, and that these propagated from the east to the
west.
After the pole group OP3,the path traverses a sparsely
populated stretch containing only undated poles from the
Iron Prince and Iron Monarch ore deposits,both in South
Australia.The next pole,IM,was obtained from metamor-
phosed mafic dykes in different parts of the Mt Isa Inlier,
and therefore represents a regional event. Because the
dykes are not hematised,IM was assumed to represent ther-
mal remanence acquired by magnetite during the last phase
of metamorphism at the Mt Isa Inlier,at 1550–1500Ma or

Geodynamic implications
As discussed by Loutit et al. (1994), the Late Palaeo-
proterozoic apparent polar wander path for Australia con-
tains prominent inflections or bends that represent changes
in the direction of plate movement and imply reorganisa-
tion of stresses within the plate.A change in the stress field
can have a major impact on basin architecture through
flexure and faulting.It can also play a vital role in forming
ore deposits by mobilising mineralised fluids within basins
(Loutit et al.1994).
The bends join quasilinear segments,or tracks,which
can be approximated on the globe by arcs of small circles
or,more accurately,by a sequence of small,near-concentric
arc elements. Polar wander along such a track therefore
corresponds to a rotation about the axis that passes through
the centres of the earth and the small circle.In the normal
geographic reference frame where it is the plate rather than
the geographic pole that moves,the movement is a rotation
about the same axis but in opposite sense to the apparent
polar wander.
Five tracks (T) and five bends (B) are identified on the
apparent polar wander path between the Lochness
Formation overprint pole LNSO2 and the upper Balbirini
Dolomite pole BDBU (Figure 17), and at least two tracks
and three bends are likely between BDBU and the pole
group OP4.(The two poles that pre-date LNSO2 are too few
to reliably define what may be a complex older part of the
apparent polar wander path.) As discussed by Southgate
et al.(2000),most of the apparent polar wander path bends Figure20 Distribution of1750–1700Ma volcanics (filled symbols)

CONCLUSIONS
Ten new primary poles reinforce and extend the Late
Palaeoproterozoic–earliest Mesoproterozoic apparent
polar wander path for northern Australia.Concurrently,a
detailed time calibration has become available for the
apparent polar wander path from new and recently
published U–Pb zircon SHRIMP dates for nine of the form-
ations that have yielded primary poles.These dates help to
develop the apparent polar wander path into a powerful tool
for the study of one of the most important periods of
Proterozoic mineralisation in Australia. Applications
include dating,correlation and tracing of the pathways of
